You are triaging GitHub issues in the repo missingbulb/Claudinite, following the "single-issue-triage" procedure below EXACTLY. This is a read-mostly triage pass with occasional write actions (label/comment/close) via GitHub MCP tools only — do NOT use gh CLI (not available), do NOT push code, do NOT open/modify any PR or branch.

The local git working tree at /home/user/Claudinite is checked out at the exact current `main` HEAD (commit 2f89ecd), clean, with no local changes — use Read/Grep/Glob on it directly to verify "is this implemented in main now" claims. This is the authoritative, current state of main.

=== single-issue-triage procedure (verbatim) ===

Triage ONE open issue and take the FIRST applicable action from this list, in order. Every action defaults to the reversible option when the check is inconclusive.

1. **Already implemented in `main`** → **close** (state_reason `completed`) + a one-line comment citing where it landed (file/function/behavior, checked in the actual current main tree — never inferred from a linked PR merging or the issue "looking done").
2. **Conflicts with a current guideline** → label `needs-decision` + a comment naming the conflict (cite the guideline/rule it conflicts with).
3. **Blocked by another issue** → label `blocked` + a comment `blocked by #N`.
4. **Small and quick to do** → label `quick-win` + a comment scoping it briefly.
5. **Else** → leave it alone (no action).

Every checkbox in the issue body ticked is the author's own claim the work is done — the strongest completion signal, but still just a claim: use it as a reason to run the "implemented in main" check, never as the answer by itself. Verified → close. Not verified → comment naming what's still missing (don't close). A PARTIALLY-ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage as if it carried no boxes. Where the ask has no repo-side artifact (a console setting, something only a human can do), the author's own ticks ARE the closing condition — say so and close.

"Implemented in main" means the issue's actual ask is true of main's CURRENT content — confirm it there (read the actual files/code) and cite specifically what you found. If you can't point to it concretely, comment, don't close. Create the label first (via issue_write or similar) if it doesn't already exist on the repo — but in practice these labels (needs-decision, blocked, quick-win) typically already exist; just try applying it.

Return `{ action, note }` where action is one of: closed / needs-decision / blocked / quick-win / left / unchanged.

**Never re-post a verdict you already posted.** Before writing anything, read the issue's existing comments (mcp__github__issue_read method get_comments) and find the most recent comment that ends with a marker line like `<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=... -->` (a marker this same triage process posts) — or, for an issue triaged before the marker existed, judge by wording that it's a prior triage verdict. If the action you are about to take is the SAME action that comment already announced, POST NOTHING, CHANGE NOTHING (don't even re-apply a label that's already there), and return `{ action: 'unchanged', note: '<action> since <date of that comment>' }`. Closing is never a repeat (it changes state), so if your verdict is "close" and it isn't already closed, close it regardless of prior comments.

End every comment you post with this marker, alone on the last line:
```
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
```
(where `<action>` is one of: closed/needs-decision/blocked/quick-win)

=== End of procedure ===

Use these GitHub MCP tools (owner=missingbulb, repo=Claudinite):
- mcp__github__issue_read (method: get, get_comments, get_labels) to read
- mcp__github__issue_write to close an issue (state: closed, state_reason: completed) or to add/set labels
- mcp__github__add_issue_comment to post a comment
- mcp__github__get_label / list labels if needed to check a label exists (or just attempt issue_write with the label and see if it errors)

=== Your batch: triage these issue numbers in missingbulb/Claudinite ===

1323 1322 1321 1320 1313 1300 1137 1298 1174

For EACH issue number above, independently run the full procedure. Do not skip any. Be careful and accurate — verify "implemented in main" claims for real against the actual current file contents in /home/user/Claudinite, don't guess.

When you're done, report back a compact table: for each issue number, the action taken and a one-line note. This report is the sole thing I need — nothing else.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

We hit the same wall from the other side (Desktop scheduled tasks, 6 machines), and there is one property of the platform that may unblock you without waiting on Anthropic.

Approvals are stored **on the scheduled task**, not on the run and not on the settings file. The app says so in its own `create_scheduled_task` / `update_scheduled_task` tool result:

> Tool approvals granted during a run are stored on the task and auto-applied to future runs.

So for a prompt that a scheduler cannot click, the workaround is to click it **once, by hand, on a task you then never throw away**:

1. create the routine task once and run it manually ("Run now") with a human present — approve the Workflow opt-in there;
2. from then on never create a fresh task for that job. Re-point the same warm task at new work with `update_scheduled_task(taskId=…, prompt=…, description=…, fireAt=…)`. Measured on our side today: the update path raises no dialog at all, and a one-time task fires immediately (the several-minute dispatch delay applies only to recurring ones);
3. if you worry the reused task shows up under a stale name — have the seed prompt call `set_session_title` on its first turn. Verified: the session then appears under its real name (`titleSource: tool`).

The catch worth knowing before you build on it: it is per-task and invisible. A new task is cold and re-asks for everything, and nothing tells you which of your tasks are cold until one stalls. That part is auditable from disk — each task-spawned session records `scheduledTaskId` and `permissionMode` in `local_.json` next to the task store, so a nightly check can name the tasks that will stall before they do: https://gist.github.com/tonydzi/64183d29eeaa37d7b38a3775012a8c1d (stdlib only, read-only, CC0).

Not a fix for the gate itself — the ask in this issue stays valid. But it may move you from "blocked, waiting on upstream" to "runs unattended, with one human click per task, ever."

{"number":1341,"title":"Eliminate the task-janitor: fold its recovery into the scheduler run, its visibility into the dashboard","body":"## The problem

`task-janitor` is the third responsibility of the task machinery (scheduler creates, executor executes, janitor cleans up). Reviewing its four queue rules, none of them earns a daily agentless task of its own: each is either **harmful**, **noise**, or **already someone else's job**.

Owner's verdict, rule by rule:

**A — stale ready** (`ready` for ~2× its period → clear status, park `needs-human:action`)
> So a valid task that just wasn't executed becomes parked?? This seems like it creates more problems than fixes. And the comments are just noise.

The item is *fine*. Nothing is wrong with it except that no executor got to it. Parking it takes a healthy item out of the queue and holds its task's lane, converting a latency symptom into a permanent stop that a human must clear by hand.

**B — dead agent leash** (`agent-running` idle ≥3h → clear status, park `needs-human:decision`)
> The scheduler can identify that and make the status switch.

Structurally identical to the executor-leash reclaim the scheduler run **already** owns as job 3 of `queue/scheduler-run.mjs` — a deterministic, serialized, hourly label rule. There is no judgment in "idle past a clock bound"; it is the same shape, one label name apart, recovering in ~2h instead of ~25h.

**C — stuck dependency** (blocked ≥2 days with blockers open → comment, labels untouched)
> Another noisy comment. The block is there because it's there. No need to make a fuss.

The rule's own comment concedes it: *"Nothing here is stuck mechanically — it will proceed by itself the moment those close."* It changes nothing and posts a comment saying so.

**D — stateless repair** (open item with no state label → park `needs-human:decision`)
> If we can decide on a broken label set — the scheduler can do it by itself and mark `needs-human:failure` and move on.

A torn label swap is a deterministic label condition. `STATUS_NEEDS_HUMAN_FAILURE` already exists in the vocabulary and is the honest classification for it. This also retires the read-then-confirm dance the rule needs today (added for #1104) — a serialized hourly scheduler run does not race the executor the way a daily sweep does.

## Supporting facts

- `packs/claudinite-dashboard/model.mjs` `warningsFor()` **already independently computes all four conditions** as per-item warnings — stale-ready, agent past leash, stuck dependency, `unlabelled`. The broad-scope health review the janitor logs once a day into a run log is a strictly worse version of a surface that is already live and continuous. (Its warning text currently names the janitor; that goes with it.)
- The scheduler run already carries the reclaim machinery (`swapStatus`, the episode-boundary comment guarding against reclaim livelock, F18) that B and D would reuse.

## Proposed end state

1. **Delete** `packs/claudinite-tasks/tasks/task-janitor/` and `packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/janitor-rules.mjs`, with their tests and catalog/`built-in-tasks` wiring.
2. **B → scheduler run**: extend the existing reclaim job to the agent leash.
3. **D → scheduler run**: a stateless open item gets `needs-human:failure` and nothing else.
4. **A → dropped entirely.** A ready item stays ready; the dashboard already flags it as `serious`.
5. **C → dropped entirely.** The dashboard already carries the warning.
6. **Dashboard**: re-word the warnings that name the janitor to name what actually acts now.
7. **Legacy slot sweep**: `worker.mjs` also sweeps the retired slot mechanism's `[claudinite-task]` dispatch issues still open in members. Decide whether any remain in the fleet; if none, it dies with the task, otherwise it needs a home or a one-shot before deletion.

## Open questions

- Does anything in the fleet still hold open `[claudinite-task]` slot dispatch issues (item 7)?
- Anything that reads the janitor's run-log health line rather than the dashboard?","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1341","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","assignees":[],"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-24T13:33:15Z","updated_at":"2026-08-24T13:33:15Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":1235,"title":"Chain 1/3: force the twice-daily cron onto every member, and read it back","body":"Link 1 of #1225's execution chain. You will never see the conversation that planned this — everything you need is here.

```
Blocked-by: #1231
Model: sonnet
```

## What changed, and why this needs forcing

The scheduler cron went from hourly to twice daily (`docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md` §17): ` ,<(dailyHour+12)%24> * * *`. That is a change to a contract members' own files must satisfy — a workflow file plus a frequency vocabulary — so the nightly converge is not enough on its own to answer *"did it work on every repo?"*.

## What makes this step's world ready

#1231 closed, meaning #1230 merged. The queue holds this until then.

## The playbook

1. Drive Shepherd's `fleet-baseline` with `follow`, so it converges every member and reports per member rather than dispatching and returning.
2. For **each** member, read two things from the member's own repo:
   - its stamp's `packVersions` — `claudinite-lifecycle` ≥ `60822.2`, `claudinite-growth` ≥ `60822.1`, `claudinite-dashboard` ≥ `60822.2`;
   - its `.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml` `cron:` line.
3. The cron is member-specific. Compute the expected value rather than matching a constant: `node engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs ` for the minute, and the member's own `taskScheduler.dailyHour` (default 4) for the hours — so a default member expects ` 4,16 * * *`.

## What counts as this step having worked

Every member reads back **both** the stamped pack versions and its own correct two-tick cron.

The workflow file is the half that can lag: `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot push, so it lands through the member's `update` task apply-stage PR. A member whose stamp has moved but whose workflow PR is still open has **not** passed — note it and keep this issue open; it will pass on a later run once that PR lands.

## When the check fails

Comment what you actually read, per member, and **leave this issue open**. Closing is what releases the next link, so a failed step must not close.

A member you cannot read is a failure, not a pass. A scope-blocked or rate-limited sweep answers "all clear" in exactly the way a healthy fleet does — if a read did not succeed, say so rather than counting it.

## How it ends

Comment the per-member evidence on #1225, then close this issue as completed. That close releases Link 2.

{"number":1333,"title":"claudinite-canary-repo: the withhold lane it probes no longer exists","body":"The `claudinite-canary-repo` pack exists to rehearse one thing: the **withhold lane** — a `.github/workflows/` write diverted to `.claudinite/pending-workflows/`, carried in a maintenance PR, and moved into place by a session holding a credential the Action token does not have. Its probe workflow, its migration record's revision marker, and its README are all about that route.

#1317 retires the lane. A member's workflow files are static after adoption, so no flow computes or stages one, and nothing delivers a staged file any more. The pack's manifest now says so, but the probe still runs and still bumps a revision nobody reads a conclusion from.

Nothing depends on it, so nothing is urgent. Three shapes it could take:

- **Repurpose the probe.** Have it verify what still matters — that a member's scaffolded workflow files match the stubs `claudinite-tasks` ships, which is now the thing that can silently drift, since a converge cannot correct them.
- **Retire the pack.** Delete it, its record and its stub, and drop it from the catalog. Its premise is gone and a pack that reads as live but proves nothing is worse than none.
- **Leave it.** Cheapest, and wrong in the way the corpus keeps warning about: a mechanism that measures nothing looks identical to one that measures something.

Not decided in #1326 — widening that PR to delete a pack was the wrong place for the call.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1333","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","assignees":[],"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-24T11:22:03Z","updated_at":"2026-08-24T11:22:03Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":1260,"title":"Verify in production: a real member converges onto engine 60822.1 and then the convention-shaped packs","body":"#1246 landed on #1248. A pack manifest now takes `id`, `prose`, `badge`, `skills`, `worldRules` and `workRules` from its own directory, and a pack that declares no `detect`/`marker` carries no fingerprint. Coded rules moved into `/worldRules/` and `/workRules/`; a pack's tests moved into `/test/`, which the vendor set now drops by name.

**Why this could not be watched now.** The delivery ORDER is the thing at risk, and it only exists on a real member. A manifest with no `id` is dropped outright by a pre-convention loader — which fails that member's mount self-test and stops it converging at all, the #1004 failure shape. The guard is `minEngineVersion`: every pack version rose to `60822.1`, and the pack update flow treats a violation as a terminal rather than a "try anyway". So a member must land engine `60822.1` FIRST, and only then receive the packs.

The canary rehearsal ([run 32608725317](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32608725317)) proved the happy end state — a canon whose packs declare no `id` converges and passes a member's self-test. It proves nothing about the ordering, because the rehearsal restores the tree and never stamps: no member's `packVersions` or `engineVersion` has actually moved. That is what this verifies, on the first nightly converge that reaches one.

Original-issue: #1246
In-production-when: `missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary`'s `.claudinite/claudinite.json` stamps `engineVersion` at `60822.1` or above.
Verify: on that same member and at that same commit, read its stamped `packVersions` and its mount. Pass requires all three: (a) `packVersions.basics` is `60822.1` or above — the packs followed the engine rather than being held back or, worse, landing ahead of it; (b) `.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/worldRules/` exists in the mount and `.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/file-placement.mjs` does not — the pack tree that arrived is the convention-shaped one; (c) `.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/test/` does not exist — the vendor set dropped the test directory by name. Any of the three failing is a fail: report which, with the paths and versions actually read.
Not-before: 2026-08-24T06:00:00Z
Retry-every: 1 day

Model: sonnet

---

- **Not yet live** → push `Not-before:` forward by `Retry-every:`, clear this issue's `task:status:*` label, and leave it open. No comment; the bumped field is the record.

You are triaging GitHub issues in the repo missingbulb/Claudinite, following the "single-issue-triage" procedure below EXACTLY. This is a read-mostly triage pass with occasional write actions (label/comment/close) via GitHub MCP tools only — do NOT use gh CLI (not available), do NOT push code, do NOT open/modify any PR or branch.

The local git working tree at /home/user/Claudinite is checked out at the exact current `main` HEAD (commit 2f89ecd), clean, with no local changes — use Read/Grep/Glob on it directly to verify "is this implemented in main now" claims. This is the authoritative, current state of main.

=== single-issue-triage procedure (verbatim) ===

Triage ONE open issue and take the FIRST applicable action from this list, in order. Every action defaults to the reversible option when the check is inconclusive.

1. **Already implemented in `main`** → **close** (state_reason `completed`) + a one-line comment citing where it landed (file/function/behavior, checked in the actual current main tree — never inferred from a linked PR merging or the issue "looking done").
2. **Conflicts with a current guideline** → label `needs-decision` + a comment naming the conflict (cite the guideline/rule it conflicts with).
3. **Blocked by another issue** → label `blocked` + a comment `blocked by #N`.
4. **Small and quick to do** → label `quick-win` + a comment scoping it briefly.
5. **Else** → leave it alone (no action).

Every checkbox in the issue body ticked is the author's own claim the work is done — the strongest completion signal, but still just a claim: use it as a reason to run the "implemented in main" check, never as the answer by itself. Verified → close. Not verified → comment naming what's still missing (don't close). A PARTIALLY-ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage as if it carried no boxes. Where the ask has no repo-side artifact (a console setting, something only a human can do), the author's own ticks ARE the closing condition — say so and close.

"Implemented in main" means the issue's actual ask is true of main's CURRENT content — confirm it there (read the actual files/code) and cite specifically what you found. If you can't point to it concretely, comment, don't close. Create the label first (via issue_write or similar) if it doesn't already exist on the repo — but in practice these labels (needs-decision, blocked, quick-win) typically already exist; just try applying it.

Return `{ action, note }` where action is one of: closed / needs-decision / blocked / quick-win / left / unchanged.

**Never re-post a verdict you already posted.** Before writing anything, read the issue's existing comments (mcp__github__issue_read method get_comments) and find the most recent comment that ends with a marker line like `<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=... -->` (a marker this same triage process posts) — or, for an issue triaged before the marker existed, judge by wording that it's a prior triage verdict. If the action you are about to take is the SAME action that comment already announced, POST NOTHING, CHANGE NOTHING (don't even re-apply a label that's already there), and return `{ action: 'unchanged', note: '<action> since <date of that comment>' }`. Closing is never a repeat (it changes state), so if your verdict is "close" and it isn't already closed, close it regardless of prior comments.

End every comment you post with this marker, alone on the last line:
```
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
```
(where `<action>` is one of: closed/needs-decision/blocked/quick-win)

=== End of procedure ===

Use these GitHub MCP tools (owner=missingbulb, repo=Claudinite):
- mcp__github__issue_read (method: get, get_comments, get_labels) to read
- mcp__github__issue_write to close an issue (state: closed, state_reason: completed) or to add/set labels
- mcp__github__add_issue_comment to post a comment
- mcp__github__get_label / list labels if needed to check a label exists (or just attempt issue_write with the label and see if it errors)

=== Your batch: triage these issue numbers in missingbulb/Claudinite ===

1224 1296 1295 1292 1264 1225 230 276 1133

For EACH issue number above, independently run the full procedure. Do not skip any. Be careful and accurate — verify "implemented in main" claims for real against the actual current file contents in /home/user/Claudinite, don't guess.

When you're done, report back a compact table: for each issue number, the action taken and a one-line note. This report is the sole thing I need — nothing else.

{"number":1160,"title":"Verify in production: an extension repo still ships to the store now the pipeline never bumps","body":"#1151 took the version write out of the `chrome-extension` release pipeline. The daily
auto-release used to patch-bump the manifest + `package.json` and push that to `main` before
packaging; it now writes nothing and instead asks whether the version already on `main` has a
release yet. The bump moved into the change that earns it (`cer/version-bumped`), and a
deliberate minor/major is a `mode: bump` dispatch calling a new vendored reusable
(`chrome-extension-bump-version.yml`).

**Why this could not be watched at merge time.** The checks are unit-tested and the vendoring
round-trip is covered, but nothing in this repo executes a GitHub Actions workflow. The changed
behaviour — "is a release due?" — only runs in a member repo, on its own schedule, after the
nightly converge materialises the new stubs. Its failure mode is silent in the direction that
matters: a wrong condition means the extension quietly stops reaching the Chrome Web Store,
with a green-looking no-op run.

Original-issue: #1150
In-production-when: `missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator`'s `.claudinite-checks.json` stamps `packVersions['chrome-extension']` at `60821.1` or higher, AND `.github/workflows/chrome-extension-bump-version.yml` exists on its default branch.
Verify: on that repo — (a) `.github/workflows/chrome-extension-daily-release.yml` carries a step named "Has the version on main been released yet?" and declares no `bump:` job; (b) the most recent "Release to Chrome Store" run that started after the converge concluded `success`; (c) no open issue labelled `workflow-failure` whose title names "Release: Daily Auto-Release" was created after the converge. PASS = all three. A run that shipped and one that reported the version already released are both passes — the assertion is that the pipeline reached a terminal state without failing, not that it released.
Not-before: 2026-08-24T02:00:00Z
Retry-every: 1 day

Model: sonnet

The reference implementation is named here because canon holds no repo list by design; if that
repo has not converged but another extension repo has, read that one instead and say which.

## For the run

1. Read `In-production-when:` against the real artifact — that repo's committed
   `.claudinite-checks.json` and its `.github/workflows/` tree. Never infer it from this repo's
   merge, a green CI run, or elapsed time.
2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: comment the evidence actually read (the stamped pack
   version, the workflow run URL and its conclusion) and close this issue as completed. Fails:
   reopen #1150 with a comment saying what was asserted, what happened instead and where you
   read it; comment here linking that; close this issue as completed — finding the fault is
   this verification doing its job.
3. **Not yet live** → push `Not-before:` forward by `Retry-every:`, clear this issue's
   `task:status:*` label, and leave it open. No comment; the bumped field is the record.

# Single-issue triage

Triage **one** open issue and take the **first** applicable action. This **acts** — but every action
defaults to the reversible option when the check is inconclusive.

- **Already implemented in `main`** → **close** (`completed`) + a one-line comment citing where it
  landed.
- **Conflicts with a current guideline** → label `needs-decision` + a comment naming the conflict.
- **Blocked by another issue** → label `blocked` + a comment `blocked by #N`.
- **Small and quick to do** → label `quick-win` + a comment scoping it.
- **Else** → leave it.

**Every checkbox in the issue body ticked** is the author's own claim that the work is done — the
strongest completion signal an issue can carry, and the one thing that puts an otherwise quiet issue
into the first rung. It is **a claim, not proof**: read it as a reason to run the implemented-in-`main`
check, never as the answer. Verified ⇒ close; not ⇒ comment naming what is still missing. A
partially-ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage the issue as if it carried no boxes.
Where the ask has **no repo-side artifact** (a console setting, a routine only a human can touch), those
ticks by the issue's own author are the closing condition — say so and close.

**"Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content _now_** — confirm
it there and cite it. **Never** infer it from a linked PR merging or the issue merely looking done. If
you can't point to it, **comment, don't close.** Create a label if it's missing. Return `{ action,
note }` (action one of closed/needs-decision/blocked/quick-win/left/unchanged).

## Never re-post a verdict you already posted

A triage comment updates the issue, and an updated issue is the next window's touched-issue
trigger — so a comment that only restates the last one wakes this task again tomorrow, and again
the day after. The verdict is the news; re-deriving it is not.

Before writing anything, read the issue's comments and find the most recent one this task posted
— by its marker, or, on an issue triaged before the marker existed, by its wording. If the action
you are about to take is the one that comment already announced, **post nothing and change nothing**
(a label already on the issue included) and return `{ action: 'unchanged', note: '<action> since
<its date>' }`. Closing is never a repeat: it changes the issue's state and ends the sequence.

End every comment you post with this marker, alone on the last line:

```
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
```

{"number":1224,"title":"Eliminate avoidable GitHub-platform assumptions from packs","body":"A census of GitHub-platform assumptions (the platform, not plain git) across the engine and every pack found 367 distinct assumptions counted once per component — 81 in the engine, 286 across the packs.

Scoping this work to the packs, and excluding `git-github` (which owns GitHub as a subject, 38 assumptions), leaves ~248 in scope. Of those, roughly 40–50 are avoidable and fall in two buckets:

**Bucket 1 — not actually GitHub assumptions (~13).** Generic-CI facts phrased in GitHub vocabulary, which the census counts only because the wording names a GitHub feature. They hold on any CI system:

- `firebase` (4) — "release-workflow variables", "workflow dispatch"
- `web-scraping` (3) — runner IP blocks, "repository secrets", commit-step durability
- `macos` (2) — secret-gated signing lane, build annotations
- `spec-driven-product` (2) — CI-gated merge, automated release cut
- `aws-sam` (1) — deploy-workflow staleness caveat
- `research-project` (1) — branch/commit/PR conventions

The fix is a phrasing pass to platform-neutral wording. No behavior changes.

**Bucket 2 — restatements of facts another pack or skill owns (~25–30).** These violate the corpus's own dependency rule ("say what A needs from B; don't re-spell how B does its job"). Repeat offenders:

- "`GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot write `.github/workflows/`" — re-explained in `claudinite-dashboard`, `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog`, `claudinite-lifecycle` when the engine's withhold lane owns it

{"number":1174,"title":"fleet-baseline can only force `update` — there is no lever for any other task fleet-wide","body":"`fleet-baseline` is the fleet's only forcing lever, and it hard-codes what it forces:

```js
// packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/tasks/fleet-baseline/force-fleet-baseline.mjs
export const FORCED_TASK = 'update';
```

Everything underneath it is already generic — `fireScheduler(gh, fullName, ref, taskId)` takes the id as an argument, and the member-side `planWake` accepts a whitespace/comma-separated list of `task` or `pack/task` ids and *creates* the standing item when one is missing. Only the constant is fixed.

So "force task X across the fleet" has exactly one route today: dispatch each member's `claudinite-scheduler.yml` yourself with `wake: X`. That needs Actions-write on every member, which is the credential `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` exists to hold and which an interactive session scoped to a handful of repos does not have. The alternative — attaching every member to the session — is per-repo manual work, which reliably does not happen.

Surfaced doing #1158's "force `usage-fold` fleet-wide" step. It cost nothing there: the converge `fleet-baseline` forces lands a commit on each member's default branch, and that commit is exactly what `usage-fold`'s movement precondition gates on, so forcing `update` forced the fold one hop later by accident. The next task that wants a fleet-wide force will not be so lucky.

**Shape of the fix** (the lever's `README` already documents the parameter-bag pattern this would join): a `WAKE` context parameter beside the existing `REPOS` / `DRY_RUN` / `INCLUDE_DORMANT`, defaulting to `update` so every existing item keeps its meaning, passed through to `fireScheduler` and named in the run summary. The summary line already reads *"Asked each covered member's own `claudinite-scheduler.yml` to wake its `update` item"* — it would just stop being a constant.

Two things to get right, both learned the hard way in this repo:

- **The protocol spans repos.** The dispatch input is read by each member's own vendored scheduler stub, so a new spelling has to be one every fielded stub already understands. `wake` itself is unchanged here — only which id travels in it — so this should be safe, but it is the class of change that broke Shepherd's only caller in #929.
- **A parameter that stops being read must fail loudly** (#974). If `WAKE` is added, an item naming a task no declared pack owns must land in the summary's `failed` list, not dispatch `update` silently because the name did not resolve.

[{"id":5379959696,"body":"## Finding: the elimination premise does not survive contact with the files

I read every candidate site rather than working from the census summaries. **Close to none of the ~40–50 is safely eliminable.** The estimate in the issue body was derived from sweep summaries, which record *that* a pack asserts a GitHub fact but not *whether* the assertion is gratuitous. Reading them in context, almost every one is either already platform-neutral or load-bearing.

### Bucket 1 was largely a census artifact, not prose to fix

The sweeps counted the *concept* landing on Actions in practice, not GitHub vocabulary in the text. Checked line by line:

| Site | Text | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `firebase/skills/create-release-plan/SKILL.md:28,30` | "release-workflow variables", "the release workflow fails if any injected variable is unset" | already neutral |
| `macos/RULES.md:64,77` | "signing secrets being present", "in a build annotation" | already neutral |
| `spec-driven-product/RULES.md:56,127` | "gate the merge from CI", "cuts from `main`" | already neutral |
| `aws-sam/RULES.md:17` | "the last green deploy workflow" | already neutral |
| `web-scraping/RULES.md:59,154` | datacenter-IP blocks, commit-step durability | already neutral |
| `research-project/RULES.md:380` | "branch/commit/PR conventions" | cross-forge |

Genuine edits available: **1–2 marginal ones** (`firebase:50` "a workflow dispatch", `web-scraping:55` "repository secrets"), each worth one census point and each slightly *less* precise afterward. `macos/README.md:63` names GitHub Actions in a **provenance** note about a real project that genuinely used it — vaguening a factual attribution makes the doc worse, not more portable.

### Bucket 2: every candidate has a legitimate defense

- **Vendored stubs** (`chrome-extension`, `static-website` bump-version workflows) travel into member repos, where a canon reference dangles. Must stay self-contained.
- **Migration records** (`claudinite-fleet-sheepdog` ×2) are dated historical accounts. The canon says do not change historical records.
- **`task.md` files** (`claudinite-lifecycle`, `tidy-repo`, `jwt`, `product-wiki`) are read standalone by executor sessions.
- **The canary README** — the fact *is* the pack's reason to exist.
- **`claudinite-dashboard`** (`README.md:498`, `pack.mjs:37`) states the fact as the **premise** of a design decision (seed the workflow; follow the scheduler rather than `push`). It does not re-spell the withhold mechanism, and the canon rule permits A to say what it needs from B.
- **Squash-merge "restatements"** turned out not to exist: `basics` has none, and `tidy-repo/skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md:11` is a six-word parenthetical justifying its own decision rule.

### The always-loaded surface is already clean

`RULES.md` is the only text every session in every declaring repo pays for, and it is already lean: `tidy-repo/RULES.md` has **zero** GitHub mentions despite 11 credited assumptions (they live in skills and `task.mjs`, where they belong), and `basics/RULES.md`'s nine are the issue→branch→PR lifecycle itself, already delegating procedure to `git-github-advanced`.

### One genuinely ambiguous case, resolved against editing

`writing-tasks/SKILL.md:171` says `task.md` must state the **constraint** and drop the mechanism. The tracker cluster's "creation always lands an issue open and ignores a `state: closed` argument" is mechanism by that reading — but it is precisely what stops a session collapsing the two calls into one. Dropping it trades a census point for a live failure mode.

### Recommendation

**Do not run the sweep.** Landing ~40 edits to hit a number would vaguen accurate provenance, weaken standalone-readable task specs, and rewrite historical migration records — a net loss against a metric that was never a cost. The ~200 inherent assumptions are what these packs *do*; the only real lever is a forge-abstraction seam, which #959's standing decision rejects absent a second consumer.

No code changes pushed. Awaiting a decision on whether to close this as not-planned.

You are triaging GitHub issues in the repo missingbulb/Claudinite, following the "single-issue-triage" procedure below EXACTLY. This is a read-mostly triage pass with occasional write actions (label/comment/close) via GitHub MCP tools only — do NOT use gh CLI (not available), do NOT push code, do NOT open/modify any PR or branch.

The local git working tree at /home/user/Claudinite is checked out at the exact current `main` HEAD (commit 2f89ecd), clean, with no local changes — use Read/Grep/Glob on it directly to verify "is this implemented in main now" claims. This is the authoritative, current state of main.

=== single-issue-triage procedure (verbatim) ===

Triage ONE open issue and take the FIRST applicable action from this list, in order. Every action defaults to the reversible option when the check is inconclusive.

1. **Already implemented in `main`** → **close** (state_reason `completed`) + a one-line comment citing where it landed (file/function/behavior, checked in the actual current main tree — never inferred from a linked PR merging or the issue "looking done").
2. **Conflicts with a current guideline** → label `needs-decision` + a comment naming the conflict (cite the guideline/rule it conflicts with).
3. **Blocked by another issue** → label `blocked` + a comment `blocked by #N`.
4. **Small and quick to do** → label `quick-win` + a comment scoping it briefly.
5. **Else** → leave it alone (no action).

Every checkbox in the issue body ticked is the author's own claim the work is done — the strongest completion signal, but still just a claim: use it as a reason to run the "implemented in main" check, never as the answer by itself. Verified → close. Not verified → comment naming what's still missing (don't close). A PARTIALLY-ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage as if it carried no boxes. Where the ask has no repo-side artifact (a console setting, something only a human can do), the author's own ticks ARE the closing condition — say so and close.

"Implemented in main" means the issue's actual ask is true of main's CURRENT content — confirm it there (read the actual files/code) and cite specifically what you found. If you can't point to it concretely, comment, don't close. Create the label first (via issue_write or similar) if it doesn't already exist on the repo — but in practice these labels (needs-decision, blocked, quick-win) typically already exist; just try applying it.

Return `{ action, note }` where action is one of: closed / needs-decision / blocked / quick-win / left / unchanged.

**Never re-post a verdict you already posted.** Before writing anything, read the issue's existing comments (mcp__github__issue_read method get_comments) and find the most recent comment that ends with a marker line like `<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=... -->` (a marker this same triage process posts) — or, for an issue triaged before the marker existed, judge by wording that it's a prior triage verdict. If the action you are about to take is the SAME action that comment already announced, POST NOTHING, CHANGE NOTHING (don't even re-apply a label that's already there), and return `{ action: 'unchanged', note: '<action> since <date of that comment>' }`. Closing is never a repeat (it changes state), so if your verdict is "close" and it isn't already closed, close it regardless of prior comments.

End every comment you post with this marker, alone on the last line:
```
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
```
(where `<action>` is one of: closed/needs-decision/blocked/quick-win)

=== End of procedure ===

Use these GitHub MCP tools (owner=missingbulb, repo=Claudinite):
- mcp__github__issue_read (method: get, get_comments, get_labels) to read
- mcp__github__issue_write to close an issue (state: closed, state_reason: completed) or to add/set labels
- mcp__github__add_issue_comment to post a comment
- mcp__github__get_label / list labels if needed to check a label exists (or just attempt issue_write with the label and see if it errors)

=== Your batch: triage these issue numbers in missingbulb/Claudinite ===

1119 1050 1096 1112 1113 1106 1073 748 722

For EACH issue number above, independently run the full procedure. Do not skip any. Be careful and accurate — verify "implemented in main" claims for real against the actual current file contents in /home/user/Claudinite, don't guess.

When you're done, report back a compact table: for each issue number, the action taken and a one-line note. This report is the sole thing I need — nothing else.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

{"number":1296,"title":"Withheld-workflow deadlock: a member whose endpoint token is not yet stamped can never deliver the workflow that would stamp it","body":"Confirmed on `missingbulb/hitbut` (missingbulb/hitbut#102), stuck since 2026-08-21.

## The loop

1. The agent session is started by `engine/scheduler/queue/invoke.mjs`, which reads the endpoint token out of **the executor job's env** (`env[endpoint.tokenEnv]`).
2. That variable reaches the job only from `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml`, stamped below the `# claudinite:secrets` marker by the wiring converge.
3. The converge **cannot write** `.github/workflows/` — the Actions `GITHUB_TOKEN` is refused there, and the refusal rejects the whole ref — so `updates/pack-update.mjs` withholds the file into `.claudinite/pending-workflows/`.
4. The **only** thing that delivers a staged workflow is the agentic apply stage, `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/tasks/update/task.md`. Nothing in `engine/` or `updates/` moves it — I grepped every consumer of `PENDING_DIR`.
5. The agent cannot start, because of (1).

So a member that reaches step 3 with an **unstamped** token can never reach step 4. It is not slow, it is not retrying — it is permanently wedged, and no converge, no wake, no force, and no `fleet-baseline` can move it. Only a credential that may write `.github/workflows/` — a human push or a human-merged PR — breaks it.

## Who is exposed

Any member whose live `claudinite-executor.yml` predates the stamping of an invocation endpoint token it now needs. That is not a one-off: it is the ordinary state of every member between "the endpoint gets configured" and "the next apply stage delivers the workflow" — and the deadlock is precisely that the second never happens if the first is what the agent needed.

On `hitbut` the correct file has been sitting in `.claudinite/pending-workflows/` with the right line in it the whole time.

## It is also undiagnosable as written

`invoke.mjs:105-110` observes an empty env var and reports:

> the Actions secret `CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN` for invocation endpoint "default" is not set in this repo

That asserts a cause the code cannot see. The secret was set the whole time; the workflow simply never passed it. I read the message, believed it, and filed the wrong fix — the owner caught it. Anyone reading that message goes to the Secrets page, sees the secret present, and has nowhere to go next.

The message should say what was observed and name both causes, e.g.:

> `CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN` is empty in this job. Either the repository secret is not set, **or** `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml` does not pass it — check for an undelivered `.claudinite/pending-workflows/claudinite-executor.yml`, which is the usual cause.

## Worth deciding

- **Break the loop in code.** The staged→live move is a file rename with no judgment in it; the reason it is agentic is the *credential*, not the decision. Is there a lane that can deliver it without an agent — the maintenance PR itself carrying the move, for a human to merge, so the deadlock degrades to "waiting on a human" instead of "wedged forever"?
- **Detect it.** A member with a non-empty `.claudinite/pending-workflows/` that has not shrunk in N days is a wedged member by definition. `fleet-roster` already reads member trees; this is one existence check away and would have caught `hitbut` on day one.
- **Fix the message** at `invoke.mjs:110` regardless — it is cheap and it is what cost the diagnosis.

I have not picked one; the first is a real design question and the second is a policy call.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1296","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","assignees":[],"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-23T16:04:00Z","updated_at":"2026-08-23T16:04:00Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":true,"sub_issues_summary":{"total":1,"completed":1,"percent_completed":100},"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":1295,"title":"A member whose Actions jobs cannot start has no escalation path — report-failure dies with everything else","body":"Found while diagnosing why `missingbulb/missingbulbwebsite` had not converged since 2026-08-21 (missingbulb/MissingBulbWebsite#217).

## The gap

`claudinite-scheduler.yml`'s `report-failure` job exists so that a scheduled run going red reaches a human — a scheduled run reaches no one otherwise. But it is an ordinary job on an ordinary runner, `needs: [scheduler-run, drain]`, in the same repository as the thing that failed.

So when the failure mode is **"this repo cannot start Actions jobs at all"** — a spending limit, Actions disabled, a runner the repo cannot get — `report-failure` fails for exactly the same reason, in the same ~3 seconds, and files nothing. The louder the breakage, the quieter the escalation.

Observed on `missingbulbwebsite`: ~30 consecutive hourly runs, `scheduler-run` failure + `report-failure` failure + `drain` skipped, no steps, no logs, no issue filed, for over two days. The mount froze on 2026-08-21 and nothing in that repo said a word.

This is not hypothetical elsewhere either — it is the general shape of any escalation that depends on the resource it is reporting the loss of.

## What did notice

Only the fleet enforcer, from **outside** the repo: `fleet-roster`'s drift issue (missingbulb/Shepherd#95), open since 2026-08-20. That is the right instinct — self-maintenance cannot detect its own absence — but a drift issue is a standing report nobody is paged by, and it sat for three days.

Since #1294, `fleet-baseline` now **fails its run** when a dispatched member does not reach canon's versions, which gives that observation teeth for the first time. This issue is about whether the member-side half should stop pretending it can self-report.

## Worth deciding

- Should `report-failure` be dropped from the stub as **structurally unable** to cover the worst failure mode, leaving fleet-side detection (`fleet-roster` + `fleet-baseline`) as the honest single owner of "this member is broken"? It would also thin the workflow further, which #1289 wanted.
- Or should it stay for the failure modes it *can* report (a task that threw, a bad token) while the fleet owns the rest — in which case its own README/comment should say plainly what it cannot catch, so nobody reads a quiet Actions tab as health.
- Either way: should `fleet-roster` escalate a member that has been behind for **N days** differently from one behind by a version — a standing drift issue is clearly not enough signal on its own?

I have not picked one; the first two are a real trade and the third is a policy call.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1295","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","assignees":[],"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-23T15:43:27Z","updated_at":"2026-08-23T15:43:27Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":1292,"title":"The fleet-baseline force lever cannot deliver an engine-only content change to an already-converged member","body":"Found while forcing #1290 across the fleet. The lever reported a clean sweep — **13 fired, 6 skipped, 0 failed** ([Shepherd run 32637790192](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/actions/runs/32637790192)) — and **only 4 of the 13 actually took the change.** Eighteen minutes later the other 9 were still byte-identical to before; this is not a timing lag.

## Why

`packs/claudinite-lifecycle/tasks/update/task.mjs`:

```js
if (stamp.convergedInWindow && !(signals.sharedMount?.changedPacks ?? []).length) {
  return { run: false, reason: 'the mount converged in this window and no pack moved — nothing due' };
}
```

and `engine/scheduler/signals/index.mjs`:

```js
const convergedInWindow = commits.some((c) => c.files.some((f) => f.startsWith(`${SHARED_SUBDIR}/`)));
```

#1290 is **engine-only** — it moved no `packs/` file, so no pack version moved. Every member that had already converged this morning has `convergedInWindow === true` and `changedPacks === []`, so the precondition correctly answers `run: false`. The wake re-queued the item, the executor re-evaluated at pick, and it declined. The members that *did* take it are the ones that happened to have a pack move pending.

Nothing here is behaving incorrectly. The gap is that **there is no same-day delivery path for an engine content change that bumps no `ENGINE_VERSION` and moves no pack** — and the force lever's report does not say so. This is exactly the "counts dispatches, not outcomes" blindness the task's own header warns about (Sheepdog#172): the sweep's own output reads as a successful fleet-wide delivery.

## Observed

| Took #1290 | Declined |
|---|---|
| `claudinitecanary`, `shepherd`, `shoutsandwhispers`, `wip` | `crosswordchat`, `edfringenow`, `googlecalendareventcreator`, `hitbut`, `laughcounter`, `tldr`, `vascularcoloring` |

(`claudinitewebsite` and `missingbulbwebsite` were fired but could not be cloned to check.)

The 9 will converge at their next window, when `convergedInWindow` goes false — within ~24h. So this is a latency gap, not a correctness one. But it is a latency gap that silently defeats the one lever built to close it.

## Worth deciding

- Should `fleet-baseline` report **outcomes** rather than dispatches — i.e. read each member's stamp or mount after firing, so a sweep that delivered to 4 of 13 says so? That is the fix that makes the lever honest regardless of cause.
- Should the `update` precondition consider canon HEAD's own movement (`stamp.canonHead` is already collected) and not just pack versions, so an engine content change is "due"?
- Or is the answer simply that an engine change that must reach the fleet today has to bump `ENGINE_VERSION` — in which case that belongs written down where a session forcing a change will read it.

I have not picked one; each trades differently and the third is a standing-decision question.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1292","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","assignees":[],"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-23T12:14:31Z","updated_at":"2026-08-23T12:14:31Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}
